title: Management of Fusarium Wilt in Watermelon
key_facts: Fusarium wilt is described as one of the economically important diseases of watermelon.
The pathogen can remain viable in soil for 15–20 years in the source discussion.
Four races are described: Race 0, Race 1, Race 2 and Race 3.
FON infects roots and enters xylem, restricting water and nutrient flow and producing wilt.

races.source_note: Able to infect varieties with no specific resistance genes in the source.
Can overcome resistance present in Sugar Baby; described as prevalent in the U.S. source context.
Causes severe disease on almost all commercial cultivars in the source context.
Described as able to overcome Race 2 resistance gene; recently detected in Maryland in the source context.

symptoms: Dull gray-green leaves and wilting during the heat of the day.
Older leaves tend to wilt first; wilt can initially be unilateral.
Initially wilted vines may recover at night, later becoming permanent.
Brown streaking/discoloration in vascular tissue of lower stem and vines.
Fruit may be small, misshapen, crack or sunburn with age.
Infected plants can occur in clusters/foci that enlarge as the pathogen spreads in soil.
Symptoms can resemble other vascular wilts; testing may be needed to verify cause.
favorable_conditions: Plant-parasitic nematodes such as root-knot nematodes
Root infection favored by cool, moist spring conditions
Wilt expression most pronounced during warm, dry periods

management.title: Clean transplants
items: Discard or thoroughly sanitize seedling trays before reuse

management.title: Sanitation
items: Clean tools and equipment to prevent moving soilborne inoculum into non-infested fields

management.title: Resistant varieties
items: Source notes resistance can be overcome under high pathogen populations or favorable disease conditions

management.title: Grafting
items: Graft susceptible scion onto resistant bottle gourd or squash rootstocks
Source describes rootstock resistance as a way to prevent root infection of susceptible scion

management.title: Crop rotation
items: Long-term crop rotation is described as important because inoculum persists in soil
Source reports one study with inoculum declines of 20% after one year, 40% after two years and 50% after three years out of watermelon
Source recommends watermelon only once every five to seven years and not in the same location two years in a row

management.title: Chemical management
items: Source reports progress with fungicides; one cited study used prothioconazole through drip irrigation
Only fungicides labeled for Fusarium wilt on watermelon should be used and label directions followed
